analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal pipeline safety rules, forces operators to disclose hazards to the public, and requires valves that shut off ruptured pipelines within 30 minutes.
analysis.headline: A one-senator pipeline safety bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on August 1, 2024, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require pipeline operators to install automatic valves that isolate a ruptured pipeline within 30 minutes in areas where a break could hurt people or property. It would order the first-ever federal safety standards for carbon dioxide pipelines, ban pumping hydrogen into ordinary natural gas pipes until Congress separately authorizes it, and make operators publish safety information — what they carry, where their valves are, their incident and repair history — on public websites and send annual notices to people living near large pipelines. It would also create a public-engagement office at the federal pipeline safety agency, let citizens sue violators, and steer a federal grant program toward retiring gas pipes and non-fossil alternatives.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live or work near gas transmission, hazardous liquid, gathering, and carbon dioxide pipelines — especially in densely populated areas and communities that pipeline incidents have historically hit hardest — get faster shutoffs after ruptures, mandatory disclosure of hazards and incident history, and a new right to sue operators in federal court. Low-income communities and communities of color get targeted outreach, complaint assistance, and post-incident support from a new federal office. Local emergency responders get carbon dioxide-specific training. Utility workers get grant-funded training favored by prevailing-wage and apprenticeship rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near pipelines and local responders

how_it_helps.text: Operators of pipelines six inches or larger in high-consequence areas would have to fully isolate a ruptured segment within 30 minutes of detecting the rupture, and existing pipelines would get five years to prove they can comply; waivers require demonstrating infeasibility, consulting the public, and expire after five years.

The bill would require the first federal minimum safety standards for carbon dioxide pipelines — including leak-detection odorants, fracture-propagation protection, geohazard assessment, and notification of residents in the potential impact area — responsive to the federal report on the 2020 Denbury pipeline rupture.

Operators would have to publish safety data free of charge — substances carried, valve locations, set-back distances, emergency plan excerpts, incident and repair history, and, for CO2 pipelines, modeled fatal-concentration zones — and annually notify owners, tenants, and first responders near large pipelines.

A new Office of Public Engagement at the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration would run outreach, a standardized complaint process, and post-incident support, prioritizing environmental-justice communities, with $12 million per year authorized for fiscal 2025-2028.

Citizens would gain a right to sue pipeline violators — and the Secretary for failing nondiscretionary duties — in federal court for penalties and injunctions, and the cap on civil penalties for a related series of violations would be removed.

The bill would bar pipeline operators from blending hydrogen into ordinary natural gas distribution systems until Congress separately authorizes safe regulation, while directing a federal study of hydrogen blending risks.

Members of the federal technical safety standards committees could have no financial interest in the pipeline, petroleum, ethanol, or gas industries, and regulators would be required to weigh avoiding the prolongation of fossil-fuel infrastructure when setting standards and applying new rules to existing pipelines.

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline and gas utility operators would bear the cost of installing and demonstrating rupture-mitigation valves within five years, publishing safety data and sending annual notifications, building and reporting new carbon dioxide safety measures, and facing citizen suits and uncapped civil penalties. Gas distribution utilities would also face pressure to retire rather than repair old pipe, since the grant program would direct at least 20 percent of renewed funding to non-emitting alternatives. Those compliance costs would likely be passed through to customers' utility bills over time.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for operators — retrofitting rupture-mitigation valves on existing lines, publishing and mailing safety information, and upgrading CO2 pipelines — would likely be passed on to utility customers, and the bill authorizes $1 billion in new grant spending over five years plus $48 million for the new office.

The 30-minute isolation requirement may be operationally or economically infeasible for some long or remote pipeline segments; the bill itself acknowledges this by allowing waivers, which could become a source of delay and negotiation.

The bill would prohibit hydrogen blending in natural gas distribution systems by statute rather than by evidence-based rule, potentially foreclosing one decarbonization pathway before the mandated federal study of its risks is complete.

Striking the existing cost-effectiveness provisions from pipeline safety rulemaking, as the bill does, would let regulators adopt much more expensive standards without weighing the costs passed to ratepayers, a trade-off critics of such rules commonly raise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety and disclosure provisions target real, documented risks — ruptured gas transmission lines near homes, the absence of federal CO2 pipeline standards, and residents who cannot currently get basic safety data about the pipes near them — and the waiver process and five-year phase-in limit the shock to operators. The main honest cost is ratepayer money for retrofits and information systems, plus $1 billion in federal grants, some of which supports replacing gas pipes with electric and geothermal alternatives that come with their own transition costs for gas utilities. On balance the bill is a fairly standard, if ambitious, safety-and-transparency measure aimed squarely at operators.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill in the Senate on August 1, 2024, late in the 118th Congress.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — was ever taken.
The bill drew zero cosponsors in either chamber, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline and gas utility operators, who avoided the valve retrofits, disclosure requirements, CO2 safety standards, and citizen-suit exposure the bill would have imposed. Because it never had a committee hearing or vote, the public record shows only that the committee took no action and no one else signed on.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Maria Cantwell (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred — no hearing, no markup, no report — so it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the record shows only one supporter and no recorded opposition; the Democratic-chaired Commerce Committee let it sit without action.

industries.industry: Gas and hazardous liquid pipeline operators
industries.note: They would have to retrofit rupture-mitigation valves within five years, publish safety data and annual notifications, report smaller releases, and face uncapped penalties and citizen lawsuits. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against residents' interest in faster shutoffs and disclosure.

A renewed $1 billion grant program would help them fix or retire old distribution pipes, but at least 20 percent of funds would be steered to non-emitting alternatives and prevailing-wage and apprenticeship preferences would apply, pushing utilities away from pipeline repair and toward electrification.

industries.industry: Carbon dioxide pipeline operators and the carbon-capture transport industry
industries.note: First-ever federal CO2 pipeline safety standards, odorant and leak-detection requirements, resident notification of fatal-concentration zones, and emergency-responder training would add costs to a nascent industry that currently operates under limited federal rules.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel producers (oil, petroleum, ethanol, gas)
industries.note: Regulators would be required to weigh avoiding the prolongation of fossil-fuel infrastructure when setting standards, industry members with financial interests would be barred from federal technical safety committees, and disclosure rules would expose blends and contaminants in the gas system.

At least 20 percent of renewed pipeline-safety grant funding would go to electrification, networked geothermal, efficiency, and related alternatives, with extra grant consideration for prevailing-wage and apprenticeship-compliant workforces.
